hero.title: Connecting a Resistance with an Inductor or Capacitor in Series
hero.lead: 4-6 Connecting a resistance and a pure inductor in series · 4-7 Connecting a resistance and a pure capacitor in series

objectives: Draw the voltage and impedance phasor diagram for a series RL circuit and compute the impedance and phase-difference angle.
Draw the voltage and impedance phasor diagram for a series RC circuit and compute the impedance and phase-difference angle.
Define the power factor and compute it in both circuits.

content.label: 📌 4-6 Connecting a Resistance and a Pure Inductor in Series
content.html: You learned, dear student, that the voltage across the resistance is in phase with the current, while the voltage across the inductor leads the current by a phase-difference angle of (90°); therefore the total voltage leads the current by a phase-difference angle (Ø). If we draw its phasor diagram, it will look like Figure (4-12).

content.svgAriaLabel: An interactive phasor diagram for a series resistance-and-inductor circuit
content.sectionHeading: 🕹️ Interactive simulation: the phasor diagram of a series RL circuit (Figures 4-12 and 4-13)
content.descriptionHtml: Move the \(V_R\) and \(V_L\) sliders and watch the total-voltage phasor \(V_T\) and the impedance phasor \(Z\) change with them, along with the phase-difference angle (Ø) between them.
content.sectionNavLabel: 🕹️ The Phasor Diagram of an RL Circuit

content.html:
$$ V_T = \sqrt{V_R^2 + V_L^2} $$ $$ \tan\emptyset = \dfrac{V_L}{V_R} $$

where: \(V_T\) is the total voltage, \(V_R\) is the voltage across the resistance, \(V_L\) is the voltage across the inductor; used to find the phase-difference angle.
A new factor will appear in this circuit, representing the ratio of the real power to the apparent power, called the power factor \((\cos\emptyset)\).

There is another diagram — the impedance diagram — which is the vector sum representing the combined opposition offered by the resistance and inductor against the alternating current, measured in ohms, and denoted by the symbol (Z); it is a vector quantity, as shown in the impedance phasor diagram (Figure 4-13).

$$ Z = \dfrac{V_T}{I_T} $$

(by Ohm's law)

$$ Z = \sqrt{R^2 + X_L^2} $$

(or from the phasor diagram)

$$ \tan\emptyset = \dfrac{X_L}{R} $$ $$ \cos\emptyset = \dfrac{R}{Z} $$
The resistance and the inductive reactance cannot be added arithmetically — why?

content.problemHtml: An AC circuit consists of a resistance of \((15\ \Omega)\) and a pure inductor of inductive reactance \((20\ \Omega)\), with an AC source connected in series, of potential difference \((150\ \text{Volt})\) and frequency \(\left(\dfrac{500}{\pi}\ \text{Hz}\right)\). Find: 1- The circuit's impedance. 2- The circuit's current. 3- The power factor. 4- The phase-difference angle between the voltage and the current. 5- The inductor's inductance?

content.label: 📌 4-7 Connecting a Resistance and a Pure Capacitor in Series
content.html: There is a voltage phasor diagram, as shown in Figure (4-14), from which we conclude the following.

content.svgAriaLabel: An interactive phasor diagram for a series resistance-and-capacitor circuit
content.sectionHeading: 🕹️ Interactive simulation: the phasor diagram of a series RC circuit (Figures 4-14 and 4-15)
content.descriptionHtml: Move the \(V_R\) and \(V_C\) sliders and watch the total-voltage phasor \(V_T\) lag \(V_R\) by an angle Ø (negative), because the capacitor's voltage is subtracted vectorially (downward).
content.sectionNavLabel: 🕹️ The Phasor Diagram of an RC Circuit

content.html:
$$ V_T = \sqrt{V_R^2 + V_C^2} $$ $$ \tan\emptyset = \dfrac{-V_C}{V_R} $$

(the phase-difference angle Ø)

In a resistance circuit connected to an AC source, the voltage is in phase with the current; whereas in a capacitor circuit connected to an AC source, the total voltage lags — that is, the current leads the total voltage by the phase-difference angle Ø.
From the impedance phasor diagram we conclude the following:

$$ Z = \sqrt{R^2 + X_C^2} $$ $$ \tan\emptyset = \dfrac{-X_C}{R} $$ $$ \cos\emptyset = \dfrac{R}{Z} $$

or

$$ \cos\emptyset = \dfrac{V_R}{V_T} $$

(the power factor)

$$ P = I_T V_T \cos\emptyset $$

content.problemHtml: A capacitor of capacitance \((100\ \mu F)\) is connected across the terminals of an AC source of voltage \((120\ \text{Volt})\) and frequency \(\left(\dfrac{500}{\pi}\ \text{Hz}\right)\), together with a resistance of \((10\ \Omega)\) in series. Calculate: 1- The capacitive reactance. 2- The current flowing in the circuit. 3- The phase-difference angle between the voltage and the current? Given that the circuit's frequency is \(\left(\dfrac{500}{\pi}\ \text{Hz}\right)\).

solution.label: Detailed Solution

questions.question: In a series resistance-and-inductor circuit, the total voltage relative to the current:
options: Is exactly in phase with it
Leads it by a phase-difference angle Ø between zero and 90°
Leads it by an angle larger than 90°
questions.explain: Since the resistance's voltage is in phase with the current and the inductor's voltage leads it by 90°, the total voltage leads the current by a phase-difference angle Ø that lies between zero and 90°.

questions.question: The impedance of a series RL circuit is computed from the relation:
questions.explain: Since R and X_L are 90° out of phase, they are added vectorially: \(Z=\sqrt{R^2+X_L^2}\), not by direct arithmetic addition.

questions.question: In a series resistance-and-capacitor circuit, the current relative to the total voltage:
options: Leads it by a phase-difference angle Ø
Is exactly in phase with it
questions.explain: In a series RC circuit, the total voltage lags the current, that is, the current leads the total voltage by the phase-difference angle Ø.

questions.question: The power factor is defined as the ratio between:
options: The resistance and the inductive reactance
The apparent power and the real power
The real power and the apparent power
questions.explain: The power factor is the ratio of the real power to the apparent power of the circuit, \(\cos\emptyset=R/Z=V_R/V_T\).

summary.heading: 📋 Lesson Summary
items: Series RL circuit: \(V_T=\sqrt{V_R^2+V_L^2}\), \(Z=\sqrt{R^2+X_L^2}\), \(\tan\emptyset=X_L/R\), and the voltage leads the current.
Series RC circuit: \(V_T=\sqrt{V_R^2+V_C^2}\), \(Z=\sqrt{R^2+X_C^2}\), \(\tan\emptyset=-X_C/R\), and the current leads the voltage.
The power factor \(\cos\emptyset=R/Z=V_R/V_T\) in both circuits.
R and X cannot be added arithmetically because they differ in phase; they are added vectorially (Pythagorean theorem).
